title: MA9-10395
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Mexico, is alleging a well-founded fear of persecution and that she would be subjected to a risk to her life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture should she return to her country, as per section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The claimant, who is 35 years old, alleged that she is a lesbian and that she has been discriminated against all her life because of her sexual orientation.

The claimant alleged that she met her partner, whose first name is XXXX, in 2000, in the city of XXXX, in the state of XXXX, where they both lived. She alleged that their relationship was originally clandestine, since they wanted to keep it a secret from XXXX's father in particular, because he was openly homophobic.
The claimant alleged that XXXX's father threatened to kill her in 2003, after he found out about the claimant's relationship with XXXX.

The claimant alleged that she moved to the city of XXXX, in the state of XXXX XXXX, approximately 400 kilometres from XXXX, in XXXX 2003, for her work. She alleged that XXXX joined her in XXXX 2005 in XXXX, where they then lived together.
The claimant alleged that she heard that XXXX's father had been trying to find them in XXXX and that she and XXXX moved to the city of XXXX, in the state of XXXX XXXX, in XXXX 2008.
The claimant alleged that she and XXXX returned to live in XXXX, still together, in XXXX 2009, because XXXX was undergoing artificial insemination treatments in that city.
The claimant alleged that she was in XXXX for work on XXXX XXXX, 2009, when she was forcibly confined and robbed.
The claimant alleged that a friend advised her to seek refuge in Montréal, and she left her country on XXXX XXXX, 2009, and came to Canada, where she claimed refugee protection upon arrival.
The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" for the following reasons.
Given the passport submitted as evidence,1 the panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity.
The credibility of some of the claimant's main allegations was initially assessed by the panel in this file.

When asked about her forcible confinement and robbery on XXXX XXXX, 2009, the claimant started by explaining that she was in XXXX on that day for work and that she had to collect money at the homes of a number of clients who owed money to the company that she worked for. She explained that the business was bankrupt and was in the process of shutting down.

The claimant explained that two men allegedly forced her into a car and that one of them stated that he knew her. The claimant then allegedly offered them money, and the two men accepted. She allegedly drove the two men to her hotel room to give them the money that she had collected from the clients, and the two men then left.
The claimant testified that she telephoned XXXX, who had stayed in XXXX, and she told the claimant that she had informed her mother of all the minute details of their life together.
When asked why she was attributing this incident to XXXX's father, the claimant replied that it was because the abductors knew her name.

The panel notes, however, that the claimant's testimony gave no indication that the abductors had ever mentioned anything about XXXX or her father, or anything about the claimant's sexual orientation during this incident. The panel is of the opinion that the fact that the abductors knew the claimant's name does not demonstrate that they were [translation] "sent" by XXXX's father, especially considering that the claimant had been living and working in Cancun for a number of years and that many people in that city might have known her name and what kind of work that she did.

She was also asked why she thought XXXX's father, who lives in XXXX, would have sent people after her in XXXX, where the claimant was travelling for business, more than 400 kilometres away, if he had learned that she and XXXX had been seen living together in XXXX; the claimant did not provide an answer. The panel is of the opinion that it is implausible that XXXX's father could have behaved this way considering that the claimant and XXXX lived in XXXX.
Consequently, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant has not demonstrated, on a balance of probabilities, that the incident of XXXX XXXX, 2009, happened because of her sexual orientation.

Furthermore, when asked whether there might be another part of Mexico, namely the capital, Mexico City, F.D., where she could live without fear of encountering XXXX's father, the claimant replied that she does not want to return to Mexico for fear of being discriminated against because of her sexual orientation.

The panel is of the opinion that the evidence submitted does not demonstrate that the claimant would face a risk in returning to Mexico, and even less so in Mexico City, F.D., under either section 96 or subsection 97(1) of the Act, given that the person that she allegedly fears, XXXX's father, was not able to find her for many years in the state of XXXX XXXX or in the city of XXXX, where the claimant lived before leaving for Canada.

The panel is of the opinion that the evidence submitted does not demonstrate that there would be obstacles, laws, regulations, and so on that would make it unreasonable for the claimant to settle in Mexico City, F.D.

As for the claimant's allegation regarding her fear of returning to Mexico because of the discrimination that she might experience, the panel notes that, initially, this allegation was not mentioned in her answer to question 31 of her Personal Information Form (PIF).2 The panel notes that what is actually written regarding discrimination is: [translation] "I have learned to live with this discrimination." The claimant then writes that she left Mexico because of the threats against her, which were allegedly made by her partner's father. When questioned on this topic, the claimant simply replied that she fears discrimination in Mexico.

The panel is of the opinion that the absence of any allegation in the PIF of this fear of discrimination from the general population already undermines the claimant's credibility on this subject. The panel also notes that the evidence submitted demonstrates that the claimant was not planning to leave Mexico before the alleged incident of XXXX XXXX, 2009, since she testified that she and XXXX had both obtained a passport at the beginning of XXXX 2009 in order to travel abroad after XXXX eventually became pregnant and to decide together where they would come back and settle in Mexico.

The claimant nevertheless testified about past incidents of discrimination that she endured, particularly with her father when she was young and living with her parents; in elementary school, where she had arguments with one student in particular; and in difficult jobs that she held where she earned less than other employees. The claimant also testified about an argument that she had with a neighbour in XXXX and about an incident in that city when, according to the claimant's testimony, the owner of a café asked her and XXXX to leave the establishment after they [translation] "displayed affection" for each other. She also alleged that she was insulted because of her appearance.

The panel is of the opinion, however, that the evidence submitted does not demonstrate that the incidents of discrimination or the insults-which are not mentioned in the PIF-that the claimant might have been experienced in Mexico are sufficiently significant to establish a reasonable fear of persecution or that their cumulative effect is sufficiently significant to render the claimant's life intolerable in Mexico, also considering the panel's conclusions at paragraph 24.

In light of all the aforementioned, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, the essential elements of her claim and, therefore, that she has not discharged her burden of demonstrating that she would face a serious possibility of persecution or a probability of being subjected to a risk to her life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture, should she return to her country.
The panel determines that XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection".

The panel therefore rejects her claim.
